topics.name: Airlift and supply
topics.question: How much supply reached the troops?
topics.intro: At Arnhem, dispatchers and the receiving division kept separate daily accounts. At Stalingrad, the army’s cargo receipts and the postmaster’s surviving returns cover different goods. Compare the journeys through the records each recipient kept.

cases.title: Stalingrad: getting in and feeding the pocket
cases.beneficiary: German Sixth Army, its dumps, and the soldiers they supplied.
cases.finding: On 29 November 25 of the 59 aircraft that took off landed in the pocket. The next day 66 landed out of 77 committed. A later receipt shows why cargo composition mattered. On 16 December the quartermaster recorded 125 tons, roughly two-thirds fuel, and called for bread.
cases.alternative: Weather, the loss of landing grounds, the changing size of the pocket and combat all affected deliveries. Army priorities also changed. A load that met a fuel request did little for the ration issue.
cases.limit: No matched weighed departure manifest and unit issue return was located for 16 December. A secondary daily reconstruction lists 174 tons flown in that day. Both are arrival descriptions with different provenance. The discrepancy cannot measure cargo lost en route.

cases.title: Arnhem: from the aircraft to the supply dump
cases.finding: On 19 September the division counted 21 net tons gathered from a drop it put at 388. On 20 September it gathered 41 from 386. The two headquarters broadly agree on the size of those drops, then diverge on the later lifts.
cases.alternative: The perimeter contracted and the division lost collection vehicles. By the last day it counted two serviceable jeeps and trailers. Supplies could land in British lines and be used before the divisional dump saw them.
cases.limit: The division published 106 tons collected and 7.4% for the operation. The 106 includes 14 from landed gliders on 18 September. The 1,431-ton total in appendix D covers drops. The further 100 tons suggested by the division was an unmeasured estimate. The dates and scopes do not support a single independently verified collection rate. Removing the glider cargo leaves 92 recorded tons from drops, or 6.4% of the division’s 1,431. This narrower calculation still excludes unrecorded local collections.

tables.title: What the two headquarters recorded
tables.scope: Diary estimates and divisional net tons are separate series. Unreported entries are blank in the CSV. Zero means the source explicitly recorded no drop or no collection.

rows.note: Another 14 tons came off three Hamilcar gliders and are excluded from this drop column.
The division’s 21 ÷ 388 gives 5.4%.
Two collections, 3 and 38 tons. Together they account for the division’s 10.6%.
The dispatch diary and the divisional account also differ on the aircraft count.
The dispatch diary dates Market V here. The division explicitly recorded no mission.
The division’s 23 September lift is also dated to this day in the RAF Museum chronology. The diary entry concerns freighting.
No mission in the division’s return.
Appendix D records eight tons. The RAF Museum describes aircraft returning without a ground signal. The division recorded no collection.

tables.scope: 1st Airborne Division, Part II, appendices D and E(i). Weight in net approximate tons. About 100 further tons were suggested without supporting figures and are excluded from both calculations.

Includes centrally counted collections from drops. The division reports that nearly all recovered stores were issued. Individual unit receipts are incomplete.

topics.name: Beaches and shipping
topics.question: What could the landing forces do under air cover?
topics.intro: Sicily’s western task force counted raids stopped before reaching the ships. In Normandy the fleet described little daylight opposition, then recorded very different unloading conditions on its two beaches.

cases.title: Sicily: ships could work even when attacks got through
cases.beneficiary: Troops landing in Sicily and the transports unloading in the western assault areas.
cases.finding: The Western naval plot distinguishes raids driven off from raids that entered the assault areas. At Gela, Captain Harwood reported that Joseph T. Dickman could keep unloading through attacks. Near misses forced a short shift of anchorage. The ship finished unloading on the afternoon of 11 July. The ammunition ship Robert Rowan was lost the same day.
cases.alternative: Harwood credited his crew and sent men ashore when the Army shore party was diverted to defend the beach. Shore fighting and unloading arrangements also governed the pace.
cases.limit: The naval plot omits low raids it could not track. No. 92 Squadron’s record of patrols over Pachino documents a different sector. Neither account supplies an estimate of ships that would have been lost without cover.

tables.title: What reached the western assault areas
tables.scope: US naval operations-board plots, from 02:45 on 10 July to 18:15 on 12 July. The unit is a raid, potentially involving multiple aircraft.

rows.note: The latter two counts partition the first. Most raids that entered were engaged. Late detection left further raids outside the plot.

cases.title: Normandy: cover overhead, different results on the beaches
cases.beneficiary: Shipping and landing forces off Utah and Omaha, with a separate Canadian view from Juno.
cases.finding: The Western Naval Task Force recorded its fighter cover in place on D-Day and slight enemy activity after dark. Utah was unloading efficiently by 7 June and Omaha by 8 June. On the eastern beaches, a Canadian pilot remembered four patrols while an infantryman coming ashore at Juno described taking machine-gun fire.
cases.alternative: Under the same western air cover, Omaha faced obstacles, stranded craft and fire at the exits. At Utah unloading was already proceeding on schedule. On 10 June weather interrupted afternoon cover for 42 minutes.
cases.limit: The naval commander credited the deterrent effect of the fighters. The reports establish that ships worked and describe the threats they faced. They cannot count attacks averted or assign an extra ton of supplies to a particular patrol.

tables.title: Separate role returns from beach-cover strength
tables.scope: Western Task Force flagships originated or relayed these direct-support missions. Beach patrols were a separate task.

rows.note: The fleet recorded night minelaying, flares and reconnaissance. Its report covers the western sector.
The 14:05–14:47 break refers to fighter cover. These daily direct-support totals cannot be attributed to that break.

topics.name: Industry and replacement
topics.question: How long did industrial disruption last?
topics.intro: Recovery took different forms. Bearing stocks cushioned factory losses. Synthetic fuel remained scarce. Fighter output recovered while operational strength and serviceability followed their own course.

cases.title: Schweinfurt: a factory loss that stocks could absorb
cases.beneficiary: German bearing producers and manufacturers using their output.
cases.finding: Schweinfurt’s September output fell to 35% of its pre-raid level. Production recovered to the pre-raid level by autumn 1944 in the survey’s wider industry account. Its investigators could establish no measurable loss of essential finished war production attributable to the bearing shortage.
cases.alternative: Users drew down stocks, changed components and obtained bearings from other sources. Many machine tools survived damage to buildings.
cases.limit: The September percentage describes the local centre. The later recovery statement concerns the industry. The records do not supply a continuous local series between those two points.

tables.title: Machinery and inventory at the works
tables.scope: RAF historical assessment from German records. Each percentage has its own denominator.

rows.note: Damage to machinery and existing stocks after the August attack.
Approximate stock share. Neither column describes the percentage of monthly output lost.

cases.title: German fuel: partial reopening and a prolonged shortfall
cases.beneficiary: German aviation fuel users and the people rebuilding the synthetic plants.
cases.finding: Leuna returned to partial operation about ten days after its May shutdown. Its output later reached three-quarters of capacity, then fell again. At the national level, synthetic aviation gasoline output in September was under 3% of April’s. The survey connects the shortage to further limits on flight training.
cases.alternative: Repeated disruption and repair changed Leuna’s monthly results. The loss of Romanian crude in August also affected the broader fuel economy. Crude imports and synthetic aviation gasoline belong to different series.
cases.limit: Leuna’s plant utilisation measures all its production against plant capacity. National aviation gasoline output measures tons produced. The surviving series does not trace a particular batch of fuel to a flying unit.

cases.title: Germany: replacement aircraft and aircraft fit to fly
cases.beneficiary: Aircraft factories, Luftwaffe acceptance officers and the fighter force.
cases.finding: Bf 109 acceptances fell from 725 in July 1943 to 357 in December. In 1944 the published fighter-production series rose from 1,555 in January to 3,375 in September, despite the February offensive. At the September strength return, 71% of the single-engine fighter stock was serviceable.
cases.alternative: Factory dispersal interrupted work, then spare capacity, surviving machinery and the fighter programme supported recovery. Bad weather delayed acceptance flights. Fuel, crews and maintenance affected what units could use.
cases.limit: Monthly production is a flow; strength is a stock and serviceability a share of that stock. No linked factory-to-squadron receipt ledger was found for these national figures. A higher output cannot identify losses replaced at a particular unit.
